hero.headline: Senate rejects Republican election overhaul bill
hero.body:
The Senate has blocked the SAVE America Act, a comprehensive Republican election overhaul that President Trump identified as a top legislative priority for his party. The bill failed to advance through the chamber despite Trump's public push for passage.

The legislation aimed to implement significant changes to federal election procedures. Republican sponsors argued the measure was necessary to address concerns about election security and administration, packaging together multiple reforms into a single proposal.

The Senate vote represents another setback for the Trump administration's agenda in a chamber controlled by Republicans. Despite the party's majority, lawmakers have repeatedly blocked key administration priorities, and this defeat highlights ongoing difficulties in advancing legislation through the closely divided chamber.

Trump had pressed Republican lawmakers to make passage of the bill central to their election policy efforts, signaling its importance to his broader legislative goals. However, the measure fell short of the support needed for passage.

The outcome leaves the future of Republican election policy in question. Party leaders have not yet indicated whether they plan to attempt reviving the legislation in a modified form or will pursue election changes through other legislative approaches. The failure also raises broader questions about the administration's capacity to move its other priorities through the Senate.

The defeat comes as Congress remains engaged in other significant legislative battles. A government shutdown that began two weeks earlier continued as the Senate rejected a Republican plan to fund operations through November 21. The measure fell short on an eighth Senate vote with a tally of 49 to 45, well below the 60 votes required for advancement.

During the shutdown impasse, Democratic and Republican leaders continued to blame each other for the stalemate. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer criticized the Trump administration for approving a $20 billion bailout for Argentina while federal workers faced layoffs. "If this administration has $20bn to spare for a Maga-friendly foreign government, they cannot turn around and say we don't have the money lower healthcare costs here at home," Schumer said.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune countered by accusing Democrats of blocking government funding to extend health insurance subsidies under the Affordable Care Act. He suggested Democrats were using the shutdown strategically, saying their "political calculations are flawed."

House Speaker Mike Johnson refused to negotiate with Senate Democrats, instead accusing them of "playing games." The administration, facing pressure over military payroll during the shutdown, directed the Pentagon to use unspent research and development funds to pay service members, with troops scheduled to receive paychecks beginning October 15.

Democrats questioned the legality of redirecting Pentagon funds, but Johnson defended the move as appropriate. According to a federal workers union filing, more than 4,000 government employees were laid off during the shutdown.

cards.headline: Trump says he would be honored to meet Iranian supreme leader if deal reached
cards.teaser: President Trump said he would be willing to meet with Iran's supreme leader if negotiations produce an agreement to end the ongoing war.
cards.body:
The BBC and Guardian sources are about different stories (Labour leadership and marathon running), not about Trump and Iran.

Therefore, here is your original card text unchanged:

President Trump said he would be honored to meet with Iran's supreme leader if a deal is reached to end the war between the two countries. Speaking from the Oval Office, Trump clarified that he does not want to meet but would do so if circumstances warranted.

Trump stated he wanted to see whether negotiations could produce an agreement before committing to such a meeting. The comments came as diplomatic efforts continue to find a resolution to the conflict, which polling shows a strong majority of Americans want concluded quickly.

cards.headline: Zelensky Proposes Direct Talks With Putin in Open Letter
cards.teaser: Ukraine's president offered face-to-face negotiations with Russia while criticizing Putin's 26-year tenure.
cards.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine has called for face-to-face negotiations with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a public open letter—the first he has directly addressed to Putin since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. Zelensky argues that only direct engagement between the two countries can resolve the war.

The letter contains sharp criticism of Putin's 26-year tenure in power. Zelensky also references a recent Ukrainian military strike on St. Petersburg. According to reports, Trump has stated that both sides will need to make compromises, and Zelensky has proposed meeting in a neutral third country.

cards.headline: Hezbollah Rejects Ceasefire Agreement Between Israel and Lebanon
cards.teaser: Hezbollah has rejected a ceasefire agreement between Israel and Lebanon that was brokered by the United States and announced on Wednesday night.
cards.body:
Hezbollah has rejected a ceasefire agreement between Israel and Lebanon announced Wednesday night following U.S.-brokered talks. The Iran-backed group, excluded from negotiations, called the truce a surrender. The agreement was reached between the Israeli and Lebanese governments without Hezbollah's participation, despite the group's significant military and political influence in Lebanon.

Fighting continues despite the ceasefire deal. Israel and Hezbollah traded new strikes, with Israeli operations killing eight people in Lebanon. A U.N. peacekeeper was also killed and others wounded by mortar fire in southeastern Lebanon. Israel has indicated it will continue its ground operation in southern Lebanon despite the agreement, raising questions about whether any peace accord can succeed without Hezbollah's direct involvement.

cards.headline: Supreme Court rules against AT&T and Verizon in location data privacy case
cards.body:
Supreme Court Backs FCC Authority to Fine Wireless Carriers

The Supreme Court upheld the Federal Communications Commission's power to impose penalties against telecommunications companies, ruling 8-1 against AT&T and Verizon in a case about the agencies' enforcement procedures.

The wireless carriers challenged the FCC's system for levying fines, arguing that the agency's in-house proceedings violated their constitutional right to a jury trial. The justices rejected this argument, affirming that the FCC can penalize companies without requiring a jury to decide the case.

The case centered on whether companies have the right to a jury trial when federal agencies impose financial penalties through their own internal processes. AT&T and Verizon contended that the Constitution guaranteed them this right, but the court disagreed with only one justice dissenting from the majority opinion.

The ruling represents a significant victory for federal regulators seeking to enforce rules governing how telecommunications companies operate. The decision strengthens the FCC's ability to pursue enforcement actions against carriers without facing procedural obstacles that could delay or limit the penalties imposed.

The underlying dispute involved the carriers' handling of customer location data. The FCC had fined AT&T and Verizon for selling smartphone location information to third parties without adequate safeguards. Location data is particularly sensitive because it can reveal where people live, work, and travel, raising substantial privacy concerns about how wireless providers protect customer information.

The decision comes as privacy has become an increasingly important issue for regulators overseeing technology companies and service providers. Federal agencies have faced growing pressure to police how organizations collect, use, and share personal information. This ruling gives the FCC clearer authority to hold wireless carriers accountable for privacy violations without companies successfully challenging the enforcement process itself.

The case also has broader implications for regulatory authority across the federal government. By upholding the FCC's in-house penalty system, the court affirmed that agencies can enforce rules through their own proceedings rather than always going through the court system. This allows regulators to act more efficiently when companies violate the rules governing their industries.

The telecommunications industry has faced mounting scrutiny over data privacy practices in recent years as consumers and policymakers have become more aware of how much personal information carriers collect and can access. The Supreme Court's decision suggests that regulators will have stronger tools to address these concerns without companies being able to delay consequences through constitutional arguments about jury trials.

The decision also came as the Trump administration was in office, and the ruling backed the FCC's enforcement authority, demonstrating that the court's support for regulatory power extends across different political administrations.

cards.headline: Scientists test first vaccine designed by artificial intelligence
cards.teaser: Cambridge researchers say they have tested a vaccine created entirely through AI design for the first time.
cards.body:
Scientists at Cambridge have tested what they describe as the world's first vaccine designed by artificial intelligence. The researchers say the test represents a breakthrough in using AI technology to develop medical treatments.

The vaccine was created through AI algorithms without traditional human-led design processes. Cambridge scientists characterize the test as a world first in vaccine development, though details about the specific disease target and results of the testing were not provided.

cards.headline: US and Japan announce $1 billion science and AI partnership
cards.teaser: The United States and Japan will each invest $500 million in a joint venture focused on science and artificial intelligence research.
cards.body:
The United States and Japan have launched a major partnership focused on science and artificial intelligence, with each nation committing $500 million to the initiative. Energy Department Under Secretary for Science Darío Gil announced the agreement, highlighting it as a significant moment for scientific cooperation between the two countries.

The bilateral partnership will connect researchers and institutions from both nations to collaborate on advancing scientific research and AI development. The coordinated investment represents one of the largest joint commitments in these fields between the U.S. and Japan.

hero.headline: Armed Groups Clash in Mogadishu in Worst Fighting in Years
hero.teaser: Gun battles erupted in the Somali capital as armed groups loyal to rival politicians engaged in combat.
hero.body:
Gun battles broke out in Mogadishu on Thursday as armed groups loyal to rival politicians clashed in the Somali capital. Residents said the fighting was the worst the city has experienced in years.

The violence involved armed factions supporting competing political figures. The clashes highlight ongoing instability in Somalia, where control of the capital has long been contested among various political and military factions.

cards.headline: Ex-Wife of Dubai Ruler's Nephew Held in Custody
cards.teaser: Zeynab Javadli has had no contact with friends since Tuesday, prosecutors say.
cards.body:
Zeynab Javadli, the ex-wife of the nephew of Dubai's ruler, is in custody, according to prosecutors. Javadli had not been in contact with any of her friends since Tuesday.

Prosecutors confirmed her detention but provided no additional information about the circumstances of her custody or any charges she may face. The case has drawn attention due to Javadli's connection to Dubai's ruling family.

cards.headline: Presidential Candidate in Colombia Faces Criticism Over Soccer Jersey
cards.teaser: A Trump-endorsed candidate is accused of co-opting Colombia's national team jersey for political purposes.
cards.body:
A Colombian presidential candidate endorsed by President Trump has been accused of turning the national soccer team's yellow jersey into a political statement. Some Colombians say the candidate is co-opting the jersey, which has traditionally served as a symbol of unity in the country.

The yellow jersey is worn by Colombia's beloved national soccer team and holds deep cultural significance. Critics argue that using the jersey for political campaigning undermines its role as a unifying national symbol that transcends political divisions.

cards.headline: Mangrove Forests Recovering After Decades of Destruction
cards.teaser: Coastal mangrove forests are making a comeback, benefiting communities and climate.
cards.body:
Mangrove forests are making an unexpected comeback after suffering extensive damage from human activity. These coastal swamp ecosystems are showing signs of recovery across multiple regions around the world.

The resurgence of mangroves brings important advantages for both people and the planet. These forests shield coastlines from erosion and storms while absorbing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, making their recovery a meaningful step forward for climate resilience and the protection of coastal communities.

cards.headline: Marjane Satrapi, Author of Persepolis, Dies at 56
cards.teaser: The graphic novelist known for her memoir of growing up during Iran's Islamic Revolution has died.
cards.body:
Marjane Satrapi, the French-Iranian author and illustrator, has died at age 56. She was best known for her graphic novel series Persepolis, a landmark memoir that offered a personal account of life during Iran's Islamic Revolution and the Iran-Iraq War. The work brought her international recognition and helped reshape how the world understood Iran.

Persepolis was adapted into an Oscar-nominated animated film. According to her family, Satrapi died of sadness following the death of her husband, Swedish producer Mattias Ripa, the previous year.

hero.headline: Former National Security Advisor John Bolton to plead guilty in classified documents case
hero.body:
John Bolton, who served as National Security Advisor under President Trump, has reached a plea agreement with federal prosecutors over charges related to the mishandling of classified national security information. The former diplomat is expected to enter a guilty plea to illegal retention of sensitive national security information, according to sources familiar with the matter.

The agreement, subject to court approval, marks a significant legal development for Bolton, who held one of the most sensitive positions in the U.S. government from April 2018 to September 2019. During his tenure, he had access to some of the nation's most closely guarded secrets regarding national security, foreign policy, and military operations.

The Justice Department filed charges against Bolton in 2025 as part of what sources describe as an onslaught against the president's critics. The case underscores ongoing concerns about the handling of classified materials by senior government officials and enforcement of laws designed to protect national security information from unauthorized disclosure or retention.

Bolton's case adds to a growing list of high-profile national security officials who have faced legal consequences for improper handling of classified information. Charges of retaining classified documents carry potential penalties including fines and imprisonment, though plea agreements typically involve reduced sentences in exchange for a guilty plea.

Before his time in the Trump administration, Bolton served in various government roles spanning several decades, including as U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations under President George W. Bush. After leaving the White House in 2019, he published a memoir that itself became the subject of legal disputes over whether it contained classified information. The Trump administration unsuccessfully sought to block the book's publication.

Bolton fell out with Trump during his first administration and was ousted from his national security adviser position in 2019. The two have maintained a political feud ever since. Bolton has also been critical of Trump's recent handling of the Russia-Ukraine war. After a Trump-Putin meeting in Alaska failed to yield progress on ending the war, Bolton wrote on social media that it appeared "Putin got to Trump."

Early in 2025, Trump revoked the security clearances of more than four dozen former intelligence officials, including Bolton. Bolton was also among a trio of former Trump officials whose security details were canceled by the president.

Bolton's book, The Room Where It Happened, became a bestseller despite the Trump administration's attempts to ban its publication. In it, he detailed what he described as impeachable conduct and accused Trump of asking China to help secure his re-election.

The Justice Department has not publicly released details about the specific classified materials involved in the case. Bolton has not been detained or charged with additional crimes beyond those covered by the plea agreement.

cards.headline: Senate rejects effort to block Trump's $1.8 billion settlement fund
cards.teaser: Republicans defeated the first attempt to prevent President Trump from creating a payout fund during budget negotiations.
cards.body:
Senate Republicans narrowly blocked a Democratic amendment to prevent President Trump from creating a $1.8 billion fund to pay his allies. Democratic Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer proposed inserting language to bar the payouts into Republican-backed legislation funding Trump's mass deportation campaign.

The vote exposed divisions within the GOP, with three Republican senators joining Democrats in support of the blocking effort. The proposal has drawn scrutiny even as the acting attorney general told lawmakers the Department of Justice is not moving forward with the fund.

cards.headline: Republican election overhaul bill fails in Senate
cards.teaser: The SAVE America Act, a wide-ranging election reform measure backed by President Trump, did not pass the Senate.
cards.body:
The SAVE America Act, a sweeping Republican election overhaul that President Trump identified as a top priority for his congressional allies, has failed to advance in the Senate. The legislation sought to reshape federal election procedures and regulations.

The bill's defeat represents a significant setback for the administration's election policy agenda.

cards.headline: George Santos makes violent threat against NPR reporter
cards.teaser: The former congressman threatened an NPR journalist who reported on federal investigations into his prediction market betting.
cards.body:
An NPR reporter who investigated former Congressman George Santos's betting activity on the prediction market Kalshi received a violent threat from Santos following publication of the story. The investigation also revealed new federal investigations into Santos's conduct on the platform.

Santos subsequently denied making the threat, according to NPR's reporting. Santos was expelled from Congress and has faced multiple legal challenges in recent years.

cards.headline: Emergency caesarean births reach one in four in England
cards.teaser: BBC analysis shows a significant rise in emergency C-sections over the past five years, though no single explanation has emerged.
cards.body:
One in four births in England now involves an emergency caesarean section, according to a BBC analysis. This represents a significant rise over the past five years, showing a substantial shift in how babies are being delivered across the country.

Medical professionals and researchers are examining the reasons behind this increase, but experts say there is no single, clear explanation for the trend. The rise is affecting hospitals throughout England.

cards.headline: Scientists test first vaccine designed by artificial intelligence
cards.teaser: Cambridge researchers say they have tested a vaccine created entirely through AI design for the first time.
cards.body:
Scientists at Cambridge have tested what they describe as the world's first vaccine designed by artificial intelligence. The researchers say the test represents a breakthrough in using AI technology to develop medical treatments.

The vaccine was created through AI algorithms without traditional human-led design processes. Cambridge scientists characterize the test as a world first in vaccine development, though details about the specific disease target and results of the testing were not provided.

cards.headline: Mangrove forests recover after decades of destruction
cards.teaser: Coastal mangrove ecosystems are making a comeback globally, benefiting both communities and climate.
cards.body:
Mangrove forests are making an unexpected comeback after years of decline caused by human destruction. These swampy coastal ecosystems are regrowing across multiple regions, offering hope for both environmental and human communities.

The recovery is significant for coastal areas that rely on mangroves for storm protection and fishing grounds. These forests also help combat climate change by storing carbon dioxide, making their regeneration important for both local resilience and global climate regulation.

hero.headline: Broadcom Stock Falls Sharply on Weak AI Chip Forecast
hero.body:
Broadcom's share price dropped significantly during Thursday trading after the semiconductor manufacturer gave disappointing guidance for its artificial intelligence chip business. The stock decline erased hundreds of billions of dollars in market value, making it one of the largest single-day losses among major corporations.

The company maintained its existing AI chip sales forecast for the year while reporting software revenues that fell short of expectations. Market observers had anticipated more aggressive guidance given persistent demand for AI infrastructure throughout the tech industry. The decision to keep projections flat surprised investors who expected Broadcom to announce higher targets based on strong AI product performance in recent quarters.

Broadcom manufactures and designs semiconductors for data centers, networking gear, and AI systems. The company has profited significantly from the artificial intelligence expansion, providing specialized chips to major technology firms developing AI systems. Thursday's announcement indicated that growth in this sector may be slowing or encountering near-term obstacles.

The stock decline spread to other semiconductor companies. Shares of Micron Technology and ARM Holdings also fell, dragging the broader chip sector down. This weakness occurred despite a stronger overall market, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average gaining over 500 points. The contrast revealed investor anxiety specifically about AI chip supply chains and future demand prospects.

The disappointing results come as Wall Street reassesses how much AI-related stocks should be worth following an extended period of climbing share prices. Broadcom's market value decreased by approximately 300 billion dollars based on the day's share price movement. The company has not offered further details beyond its quarterly financial statements regarding the reasons for maintaining its AI chip guidance or the software sales shortfall.

The selloff reflects broader market concerns about whether AI valuations have become stretched. Recent weeks have brought warnings from major bank leaders that stock prices may face a significant correction after reaching record levels. Some investors and analysts have questioned whether AI investment promises will deliver actual returns, particularly given that most funding has concentrated in a small group of companies while measurable financial results remain limited.

Broadcom's earnings report adds to growing uncertainty within the technology sector. While individual company performance varies, the overall trend shows investors are becoming more selective about which AI-related businesses deserve premium valuations. The company's inability to raise its AI outlook suggests that even leading semiconductor suppliers may face constraints on growth in coming quarters, potentially signaling that the rapid expansion phase of AI infrastructure buildout could be moderating.

cards.headline: Quantinuum Closes Flat in Trading Debut After Raising $1.68 Billion
cards.teaser: The quantum computing company's stock showed little movement in its first day of trading despite raising more money than initially planned.
cards.body:
Quantinuum, a quantum computing company backed by Honeywell, made its Nasdaq debut with minimal price movement despite raising $1.68 billion in an upsized initial public offering. The company was valued at $17.63 billion at the time of listing.

The flat performance marked a subdued market reception for the highly anticipated quantum computing IPO. Quantinuum had increased the size of its offering ahead of the listing, signaling strong institutional demand for the shares.

cards.headline: SpaceX Prepares for Record IPO With Fidelity Lowering Investment Minimum
cards.teaser: Fidelity reduced barriers for retail investors as SpaceX moves forward with what could become the largest public offering ever.
cards.body:
SpaceX is moving forward with plans for a record-breaking initial public offering targeting $75 billion. The company has launched a website to reach retail investors and secured backing from major banks. Jamie Dimon is personally planning to pitch the offering to investors, underscoring Wall Street's enthusiasm for the deal.

Fidelity has reduced the minimum investment requirement for individual investors seeking to participate. SpaceX has set its IPO price at $135 per share and released a 17-minute video presentation to promote the offering to potential shareholders. The deal would become the largest IPO on record.

cards.headline: Dow Gains More Than 500 Points as Oil Prices Ease
cards.teaser: The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped to a record while the Nasdaq fell after Broadcom's earnings disappointed investors.
cards.body:
The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped more than 500 points to hit a record high, bolstered by declining oil prices that eased investor concerns about energy costs. Stocks outside the technology sector led the advance.

The Nasdaq retreated as semiconductor and AI-related stocks declined following Broadcom's earnings report and guidance. Chip makers including Micron and ARM also fell, reflecting a rotation away from the semiconductor stocks that had driven recent market gains.

cards.headline: Anthropic Co-Founder Warns AI Systems Need Controls
cards.teaser: Jack Clark said artificial intelligence could reach a point where it develops without human input, requiring safety mechanisms.
cards.body:
Jack Clark, co-founder of Anthropic, told the BBC that artificial intelligence systems require a "brake pedal" to manage their development. He cautioned that AI could advance to a point where it develops capabilities without human input or oversight.

Anthropic, the company behind Claude, has positioned itself as focused on AI safety research while developing commercial products. The firm is preparing to offer public share sales later this year, with its valuation approaching $1 trillion.

cards.headline: Meta Executive Naomi Gleit Discusses AI and Working for Zuckerberg
cards.teaser: The longest-serving Meta employee shared her perspective on artificial intelligence, jobs, and her role at the company.
cards.body:
Naomi Gleit, Meta's longest-serving employee, told the BBC she considers her current role her "dream job" despite the numerous controversies she has experienced during her time at the company. She has held various leadership positions as Meta evolved from Facebook into a major technology conglomerate.

In her interview, Gleit discussed the company's artificial intelligence work and its potential impact on employment and the broader technology industry. Her comments offer insight into Meta's internal culture and strategic direction under Mark Zuckerberg's leadership.

cards.headline: Hinge Executive Says Young Singles Need AI to Initiate Dating Connections
cards.teaser: The dating app's leader cited loneliness and lack of confidence as challenges for people in their twenties seeking relationships.
cards.body:
Jackie Jantos, an executive at dating app Hinge, argues that artificial intelligence could help young adults in their twenties make the first move on dating platforms. According to Jantos, loneliness and lack of confidence are significant barriers preventing singles from initiating romantic connections.

The comments suggest Hinge is exploring AI-powered features to assist users with starting conversations. Dating apps have increasingly turned to technology to improve how people match and communicate with each other.

cards.headline: Anthropic revenue reaches $47 billion ahead of planned IPO
cards.teaser: The artificial intelligence company reported annualized revenue crossed $47 billion in May as it prepares for a public offering.
cards.body:
Anthropic's annualized revenue reached $47 billion in May, a dramatic jump from approximately $9 billion at the end of 2025. The company is experiencing rapid growth as it prepares for an initial public offering.

Company president Daniela Amodei has downplayed concerns about returns on artificial intelligence investments ahead of the IPO. The sustainability of Anthropic's revenue growth will likely face scrutiny from potential investors evaluating the company's prospects following its public debut.

cards.headline: Airbnb CEO plans to launch artificial intelligence research lab
cards.teaser: Brian Chesky announced plans for a new AI lab after previously saying existing language model products were not ready for partnership.
cards.body:
Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky has announced plans to establish a new artificial intelligence laboratory within the company. The move reflects Chesky's previous concerns about the readiness of existing large language model products for Airbnb's specific needs, which led the company to avoid partnering with current AI providers.

By developing its own AI capabilities in-house, Airbnb aims to create technology tailored to its platform's requirements rather than adapting to available third-party solutions.

cards.headline: New iPhone and Mac app blocks ads across nearly all applications
cards.teaser: A privacy tool called Filtr now blocks advertisements from loading inside apps, not just web browsers, using new Apple software features.
cards.body:
Filtr is a new privacy tool that blocks ads across nearly all iPhone, iPad, and Mac applications. The app leverages a new feature in the latest Apple software to prevent advertisements from loading inside apps, expanding its capabilities beyond traditional web browser blocking.

This represents a significant shift in ad blocking technology, which has historically been limited to web browsing. By tapping into Apple's latest software features, Filtr now offers users more comprehensive protection across their device's broader app ecosystem.

cards.headline: Estonian benchmark tests language models against Russian propaganda
cards.teaser: The Estonian government tested dozens of AI models on their ability to resist Russian strategic narratives and disinformation.
cards.body:
The Estonian government released benchmark results showing how various large language models perform at resisting Russian propaganda. The tests evaluated dozens of AI models on their ability to combat what Estonia characterized as Russia's strategic narratives.

The benchmark examined how different language models respond to and potentially amplify or resist disinformation efforts. Estonia's evaluation comes as governments increasingly scrutinize how AI systems handle politically sensitive content and propaganda from hostile states.

cards.headline: Password manager Dashlane details breach of encrypted vaults
cards.teaser: Dashlane explained how attackers managed to download encrypted password vaults from user accounts.
cards.body:
Password management company Dashlane disclosed how attackers successfully downloaded encrypted password vaults from its service. The company provided an explanation of the breach mechanism, noting that by targeting larger numbers of users, attackers increased their chances of success.

The breach involved accessing the encrypted vaults, which store users' passwords and sensitive login information. Dashlane's disclosure focuses on the technical details of how the attack was executed against its platform.

cards.headline: Mangrove forests recover after decades of destruction
cards.teaser: Swampy mangrove forests are staging a comeback, providing benefits for coastal communities and climate.
cards.body:
Mangrove forests are making a surprising comeback after being destroyed for decades. This recovery is welcome news for both coastal communities and the environment.

The regrowth of these swampy coastal ecosystems brings multiple benefits. Mangroves act as natural barriers against storms and flooding, protecting nearby communities. They also absorb and store carbon, contributing positively to climate efforts. The healing of these forests demonstrates how ecosystems can bounce back when given the chance.

hero.headline: Los Angeles Rams acquire defensive end Myles Garrett in blockbuster trade
hero.body:
The Los Angeles Rams have acquired star defensive end Myles Garrett from the Cleveland Browns in a major trade deal. The Browns received linebacker Jared Verse, a 2027 first-round pick, a 2028 second-round pick, and a 2029 third-round selection in exchange.

Garrett, 30, is a two-time NFL Defensive Player of the Year and seven-time Pro Bowl selection. Since Cleveland drafted him first overall in 2017, he has recorded 125.5 sacks, 413 pressures, and 149 tackles for loss. Last season, he set a single-season sacks record with 23 performances, earning All-Pro recognition despite playing for a struggling team.

The trade came after Garrett requested a move from the Browns following their disappointing 3-14 season in 2024. Though he signed a four-year, $160 million extension with Cleveland shortly after his trade request, which made him the highest-paid non-quarterback at the time, the team's continued struggles prompted him to seek a fresh start. The Browns finished the 2025 season with a 5-12 record and missed the playoffs for the second consecutive year.

To facilitate the trade, the Browns and Garrett agreed to modify his contract, deferring option payments across the 2026-28 seasons. The change moved a payment of around $10 million from March 28 to the start of the regular season, enabling the deal to progress.

Browns General Manager Andrew Berry acknowledged the difficult decision in a statement. "As discussions intensified we were stuck at a legitimate crossroads: do we hold on to a truly generational player who has become the identity of our team, or do we make the difficult decision that we think is best for the organization over the long run?" Berry said.

The Rams, who lost to the Seattle Seahawks in last season's NFC Championship game, have a history of making bold roster moves. In 2021, they acquired Matthew Stafford from Detroit, and he led the team to a Super Bowl victory in his first season. That championship was won at their home SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, where next February's Super Bowl LXI will also be played.

Verse, the 25-year-old linebacker sent to Cleveland, was a first-round pick by the Rams in 2024 who earned Defensive Rookie of the Year honors. He recorded 12 career sacks and 22 tackles for loss while earning Pro Bowl selection this past season.

The acquisition creates a historic pairing in Los Angeles, as Matthew Stafford won the AP NFL MVP and Defensive Player of the Year awards last season, marking the first time these honors will belong to teammates.

cards.headline: Formula 1 extends Las Vegas Grand Prix contract through 2037
cards.teaser: Formula 1 will continue racing in Las Vegas for at least another decade after extending its contract with the city by 10 years.
cards.body:
Formula 1 has extended its Las Vegas Grand Prix contract for 10 additional years, keeping the race on the calendar through 2037. The agreement solidifies the event's place on the Formula 1 schedule well into the future.

The Las Vegas Grand Prix, which takes place on the city's famous Strip, has become an established fixture on the Formula 1 calendar since its introduction to the sport.

cards.headline: Qualifier Maja Chwalinska reaches French Open final
cards.teaser: Polish qualifier Maja Chwalinska defeated Diana Shnaider to become the first qualifier to reach the French Open final at Roland Garros.
cards.body:
Maja Chwalinska made history at the French Open, becoming the first qualifier ever to reach the tournament's final. The Polish player defeated 25th seed Diana Shnaider 7-6(4), 6-4 in an emotional semifinal performance, breaking down in tears after securing her spot in the championship match.

Chwalinska will face Mirra Andreeva in Saturday's final. Her remarkable run through qualifying and the main draw represents one of the most surprising performances in recent Grand Slam history, driven by a shift in her mental approach to competition.

cards.headline: Shakira to perform at 2026 World Cup opening ceremony in Mexico
cards.teaser: Colombian pop star Shakira will perform her official World Cup song at the tournament's opening ceremony.
cards.body:
Shakira has been confirmed to perform at the opening ceremony of the 2026 World Cup in Mexico. The Colombian pop star will perform her official song for the tournament at the event.

The 2026 World Cup will be co-hosted by the United States, Canada, and Mexico, with the opening ceremony taking place in Mexico.

cards.headline: Ollie Robinson returns to England team after 24-Test absence
cards.teaser: Ollie Robinson made his return to the England cricket team in their match against New Zealand after being left out for 24 consecutive Tests.
cards.body:
Ollie Robinson made a remarkable comeback on the first day of England's Test against New Zealand, taking four wickets for 10 runs in six overs. The 32-year-old had been dropped in 2024 amid questions about his fitness and commitment, spending time playing grade cricket for Sydney University while England struggled in the Ashes.

Robinson admitted he had feared his international career was over before this recall. His stunning performance—which included a three-wicket maiden—demonstrated the quality England had been missing during his 24-Test absence from the squad.

cards.headline: Leeds Rhinos extend Super League lead with win over St Helens
cards.teaser: Leeds Rhinos defeated St Helens at Headingley to extend their lead at the top of the Super League table.
cards.body:
Leeds Rhinos strengthened their Super League title bid with a 24-16 victory over St Helens at Headingley. The Rhinos mounted an impressive comeback after trailing by eight points at half-time to secure the win and extend their lead at the top of the table.

The result marks an entertaining contest between the two sides. Leeds' victory comes as they seek to end a long drought without silverware, having last won the Super League title in 2017.

cards.headline: British athletes win at Diamond League meet in Rome
cards.teaser: World indoor champions Molly Caudery and Georgia Hunter Bell both won their events at the Diamond League meeting in Rome.
cards.body:
World indoor champions Molly Caudery and Georgia Hunter Bell delivered impressive performances at the Diamond League meeting in Rome. Caudery claimed victory in the pole vault, while Hunter Bell won the 1500 meters with a season's best time of three minutes 58.63 seconds.

Both athletes showcased their credentials at one of track and field's most prestigious competition series, adding to their strong seasons on the Diamond League circuit.

hero.headline: Music Executive Clive Davis Released From Hospital After Respiratory Issue
hero.body:
Music industry executive Clive Davis has been discharged from the hospital following treatment for a respiratory issue, according to a representative for the 94-year-old producer. A spokesperson said Davis is "in good spirits and happy to be recuperating at home."

Davis stands as one of the most influential figures in the music industry, with a career spanning more than six decades. He founded Arista Records in 1974 and later established J Records in 2000. His work has shaped the careers of major artists including Whitney Houston, Aretha Franklin, Alicia Keys, and Jennifer Hudson. He currently serves as chief creative officer of Sony Music Entertainment.

The representative did not disclose specific details about the nature of the respiratory issue or how long Davis remained hospitalized. Despite his advanced age, Davis has continued to maintain an active role in the music business, focusing on artist development and event production.

Throughout his career, Davis has earned significant recognition. He has won five Grammy Awards and was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2000. The Grammy Trustees Award came to him that same year, and he received the Recording Academy's President's Merit Award in 2009. His 2013 memoir, "The Soundtrack of My Life," became a bestseller and offered insight into his decades in the industry.

One of Davis's most notable contributions to the music calendar is his annual pre-Grammy gala. The event has become a major fixture during Grammy weekend, attracting top-tier artists, music executives, and entertainment celebrities from around the world. In recent years, Davis has continued to host the prestigious party despite his age.

Davis's career has been defined by his ability to identify and develop talent across multiple genres. His work at Arista Records established the label as a powerhouse in the industry, while his subsequent ventures continued his track record of success. His influence extends beyond individual artists to shaping broader trends in music and entertainment.

The music industry has long recognized Davis as a visionary whose decisions and guidance have influenced countless musicians and the trajectory of popular music itself. His continued involvement in major industry events and his ongoing role at Sony Music Entertainment demonstrate his enduring influence and relevance in a field that has transformed dramatically over his six-decade career.

Davis's hospitalization and recovery add to a long list of milestones in a career that shows no signs of slowing down. His commitment to the music industry remains evident through his active participation in major events and his leadership position at one of the world's largest music entertainment companies.

cards.headline: Christopher Nolan's 'The Odyssey' Ticket Sales Crash Theater Websites
cards.teaser: Major theater chains experienced technical issues as advance tickets for the director's new film went on sale.
cards.body:
I can see that the Guardian source provided is about casting choices in "The Odyssey" and doesn't contain information about ticket sales or website crashes. The BBC source is about election results in Los Angeles and is completely unrelated to this story.

Since the additional sources don't contain confirmed facts about the ticketing system issues mentioned in the original card, I'm returning the original text unchanged:

AMC, Fandango, and Regal all faced extended wait times and website glitches when advance tickets for Christopher Nolan's upcoming film "The Odyssey" went on sale. The high demand for the film caused technical problems across multiple ticketing platforms.

The issues mirror previous instances when anticipated films have overwhelmed theater booking systems. Nolan's films typically generate strong advance ticket sales, and his previous releases have been box office successes. "The Odyssey" represents his latest project following a series of large-scale productions.

cards.headline: President Trump to Attend NBA Finals Games at Madison Square Garden
cards.teaser: The president confirmed he plans to watch the New York Knicks play in the championship series.
cards.body:
President Donald Trump confirmed he will attend Game 3 of the NBA Finals at Madison Square Garden on Monday to watch his hometown New York Knicks. He also indicated he may attend Game 4.

Presidential attendance at major sporting events requires significant security preparations and coordination with venue officials and local law enforcement.

cards.headline: Amazon and Vice Studios Sued Over 'Hollywood Hustler' Documentary
cards.teaser: A producer claims the documentary series falsely portrayed him as an accomplice to a convicted fraudster.
cards.body:
Producer Julio Hallivis filed a defamation lawsuit against Amazon Studios, Vice Studios, and director Rebecca Chaiklin over the documentary series "Hollywood Hustler: Glitz, Glam, Scam." Hallivis alleges the series falsely portrayed him as an accomplice of Zach Horwitz, who was convicted of fraud.

The lawsuit contends that Hallivis's reputation has been damaged by the implication that he participated in fraudulent activities. The documentary series examines the case of Horwitz, who was convicted of running a scheme in the entertainment industry. Hallivis claims the portrayal in the series is inaccurate and harmful to his professional standing.

cards.headline: New '60 Minutes' Executive Producer Addresses Staff Concerns
cards.teaser: The incoming leader of the CBS news program promised editorial independence following staff upheaval.
cards.body:
The new executive producer of "60 Minutes" assured staff members of editorial independence following recent personnel changes at the CBS news program. The reassurance came after correspondent Scott Pelley was removed from the show, sparking concern among team members about the program's future direction.

Three correspondents have been dismissed from "60 Minutes" in recent weeks. Former correspondent Steve Kroft remarked that the program viewers have long known no longer exists. CBS News continues efforts to stabilize the long-running news division amid these changes.

cards.headline: Steven Spielberg Predicts Discovery of Alien Life
cards.teaser: The filmmaker says humanity will encounter evidence of extraterrestrial intelligence during our lifetimes.
cards.body:
Rewrite Assessment

The BBC News source confirms the story about Steven Spielberg predicting alien discovery. However, the Guardian source is about OECD economic forecasts regarding Iran conflict impacts—a completely different story.

Since the additional source material contains an unrelated article, I'm returning the original card text unchanged:

---

Director Steven Spielberg stated he believes humanity will discover evidence of alien life within the current generation. Spielberg made the comments in connection with his new film, which explores scenarios involving the revelation of non-human intelligence.

The filmmaker has explored themes of extraterrestrial contact throughout his career, directing films including "Close Encounters of the Third Kind" and "E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial." His latest project imagines potential consequences if the existence of non-human intelligence were confirmed and made public.

cards.headline: 'Queer Eye' Star Karamo Brown Discusses Show Tensions
cards.teaser: The television personality addressed public speculation about conflicts among cast members of the Netflix series.
cards.body:
Karamo Brown broke his silence on tensions during the production of "Queer Eye," addressing long-standing speculation about conflicts among the show's cast members. Brown discussed feeling like an outsider on the Netflix series and revealed he skipped press appearances for the final season.

Brown also disclosed that he experienced a relapse during the show's production. Multiple reports characterize the behind-the-scenes environment as having difficulties, with Brown now providing his perspective on what led to a falling out with other members of the Fab Five. Brown's account differs from previous narratives about a well-known incident involving the cast.

hero.headline: Senate rejects Republican election overhaul bill
hero.body:
The Senate has blocked the SAVE America Act, a comprehensive Republican election overhaul that President Trump identified as a top legislative priority for his party. The bill failed to advance through the chamber despite Trump's public push for passage.

The legislation aimed to implement significant changes to federal election procedures. Republican sponsors argued the measure was necessary to address concerns about election security and administration, packaging together multiple reforms into a single proposal.

The Senate vote represents another setback for the Trump administration's agenda in a chamber controlled by Republicans. Despite the party's majority, lawmakers have repeatedly blocked key administration priorities, and this defeat highlights ongoing difficulties in advancing legislation through the closely divided chamber.

Trump had pressed Republican lawmakers to make passage of the bill central to their election policy efforts, signaling its importance to his broader legislative goals. However, the measure fell short of the support needed for passage.

The outcome leaves the future of Republican election policy in question. Party leaders have not yet indicated whether they plan to attempt reviving the legislation in a modified form or will pursue election changes through other legislative approaches. The failure also raises broader questions about the administration's capacity to move its other priorities through the Senate.

The defeat comes as Congress remains engaged in other significant legislative battles. A government shutdown that began two weeks earlier continued as the Senate rejected a Republican plan to fund operations through November 21. The measure fell short on an eighth Senate vote with a tally of 49 to 45, well below the 60 votes required for advancement.

During the shutdown impasse, Democratic and Republican leaders continued to blame each other for the stalemate. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer criticized the Trump administration for approving a $20 billion bailout for Argentina while federal workers faced layoffs. "If this administration has $20bn to spare for a Maga-friendly foreign government, they cannot turn around and say we don't have the money lower healthcare costs here at home," Schumer said.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune countered by accusing Democrats of blocking government funding to extend health insurance subsidies under the Affordable Care Act. He suggested Democrats were using the shutdown strategically, saying their "political calculations are flawed."

House Speaker Mike Johnson refused to negotiate with Senate Democrats, instead accusing them of "playing games." The administration, facing pressure over military payroll during the shutdown, directed the Pentagon to use unspent research and development funds to pay service members, with troops scheduled to receive paychecks beginning October 15.

Democrats questioned the legality of redirecting Pentagon funds, but Johnson defended the move as appropriate. According to a federal workers union filing, more than 4,000 government employees were laid off during the shutdown.

cards.headline: Trump says he would be honored to meet Iranian supreme leader if deal reached
cards.teaser: President Trump said he would be willing to meet with Iran's supreme leader if negotiations produce an agreement to end the ongoing war.
cards.body:
The BBC and Guardian sources are about different stories (Labour leadership and marathon running), not about Trump and Iran.

Therefore, here is your original card text unchanged:

President Trump said he would be honored to meet with Iran's supreme leader if a deal is reached to end the war between the two countries. Speaking from the Oval Office, Trump clarified that he does not want to meet but would do so if circumstances warranted.

Trump stated he wanted to see whether negotiations could produce an agreement before committing to such a meeting. The comments came as diplomatic efforts continue to find a resolution to the conflict, which polling shows a strong majority of Americans want concluded quickly.

cards.headline: House passes agriculture and FDA funding bill
cards.teaser: The House approved its second spending bill for fiscal 2027, covering agriculture, rural development, and the Food and Drug Administration.
cards.body:
The House voted 213-210 to pass the agriculture, rural development, Food and Drug Administration, and related agencies appropriations bill for fiscal 2027. Five Republicans voted against the measure, which represents the second of the annual spending bills to clear the lower chamber.

The passage marks progress for Republican leaders navigating the annual government funding process while managing competing legislative priorities. The narrow margin reflects ongoing divisions within the GOP caucus over spending levels and policy riders attached to appropriations legislation.

cards.headline: Three Republican senators vote to bar Pulte from dual intelligence role
cards.teaser: Senators Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, and Bill Cassidy joined Democrats in supporting an amendment to prevent Bill Pulte from serving simultaneously as temporary intelligence director and housing finance chief.
cards.body:
Three Republican senators crossed party lines Thursday to support a Democratic amendment barring Bill Pulte from holding both his current role as director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency and a temporary position as director of national intelligence. Senators Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, and Bill Cassidy of Louisiana voted for the measure, reflecting concern about dual leadership of the agencies.

Pulte was appointed to the intelligence role earlier this week. Trump has suggested Pulte will investigate election claims while serving as the country's top intelligence official, though the president characterized the appointment as temporary.

cards.headline: Justice Department indicts 14 in Ohio fraud scheme
cards.teaser: Federal prosecutors charged 14 state employees with stealing more than $50 million in government funds as part of a statewide crackdown on fraud.
cards.body:
The Department of Justice announced indictments against 14 people accused of stealing more than $50 million in government funds through a fraud scheme involving Ohio state employees. Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche unveiled the charges at a news conference in Columbus alongside FBI Director Kash Patel.

The indictments were part of a broader statewide effort to combat fraud in Ohio. The alleged scheme involved the misappropriation of government money by individuals working within state agencies, though the specific mechanisms of the fraud were detailed in the sealed charging documents.

cards.headline: Arizona attorney general to seek new indictments in fake elector case
cards.teaser: Arizona's attorney general will present the 2020 fake elector case to a grand jury again after the state supreme court declined to revive previous charges.
cards.body:
Arizona's Democratic Attorney General Kris Mayes said her office will present the fake elector case to a grand jury for fresh indictments. The move comes after the state's supreme court denied her appeal to revive the original prosecution against individuals accused of posing as legitimate electors for Donald Trump in 2020, despite Joe Biden's victory in the state.

The decision represents another legal setback for Mayes as she attempts to advance the sprawling case through courts. The prosecution targets Trump's former chief of staff Mark Meadows, former New York City mayor Rudy Giuliani, and others involved in the alleged scheme.

cards.headline: US and Japan announce $1 billion science and AI partnership
cards.teaser: The United States and Japan will each invest $500 million in a joint venture focused on science and artificial intelligence research.
cards.body:
The United States and Japan have launched a major partnership focused on science and artificial intelligence, with each nation committing $500 million to the initiative. Energy Department Under Secretary for Science Darío Gil announced the agreement, highlighting it as a significant moment for scientific cooperation between the two countries.

The bilateral partnership will connect researchers and institutions from both nations to collaborate on advancing scientific research and AI development. The coordinated investment represents one of the largest joint commitments in these fields between the U.S. and Japan.
